idiom_name: early return with if; throw for invalid input
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no guard keyword, but return is a core statement that ends execution immediately - MDN documents the effect as well as the automatic-semicolon-insertion trap - so the guard is the familiar if (!ok) return; at the top of the function. Invalid input at a module or API boundary exits by throwing a TypeError/RangeError (or a custom Error subclass), while internal checks return early with a default. Optional chaining (?.) and nullish coalescing (??) shrink the test expression but are not guards: they skip a dereference and let the function continue.
pitfalls: Automatic semicolon insertion turns a return whose value sits on the next line into return undefined; keep the expression on the return line.
A return inside try runs after the finally block, and a return inside finally swallows the in-flight exception.
Truthiness guards reject legitimate 0, "" and false values; when the value can be falsy and valid, test for null/undefined explicitly (x == null).
